title: Invoicing service: money and ordering helpers, behaviour notes before the 2.0 refactor
context: Engineering note drafted by a backend developer on the invoicing team for the tech lead and the two reviewers of the 2.0 refactor. It records how the current helper functions behave so the refactor can keep or deliberately change that behaviour. Snippets are in the appendix; some were run on the author's laptop and the terminal output pasted, others were not run.

claims.text: format_invoice_total() pads the amount to twelve characters.
split_instalments(1000, 3) returns [334, 333, 333], which sums back to 1000.
apply_vat() rounds each line before summing.
In by_amount, INV-1 comes first, and among invoices with equal amounts the lower invoice number always comes first.
classify runs unchanged on every Python 3 release from 3.8 onward.
round(2.5) returns 3 on the logged interpreter.
Because the default list is shared between calls, the second call add_line("B") returns ['A', 'B'].
dedupe([1, True, 1.0]) returns [1, True, 1.0].
On the interpreter in the S2 log, sum(items) == 1.0 evaluates to True.
round_money(0.125) returns 0.13.
dedupe_fast(data) returns [3, 1, 2], the same list in the same order as dedupe(data).
-7 % 2 is 1, so x % n is never negative for any integers x and n.
-7 // 2 evaluates to -3.
In the benchmark run, dedupe_fast was about three times faster than dedupe on one million items.
math.fsum(items) returns exactly 1.0, so math.fsum gives the exact decimal total for any list of amounts.
Every split_instalments call shown in S4 returns parts that differ from each other by at most one cent.
split_instalments always returns n parts that sum to the total, for any total and any n.
a is b evaluates to False, so the two calls return separate lists.
max(invoices, key=amount) returns ('INV-2', 200).
dedupe removes duplicates from any list while keeping first-occurrence order.
The retry queue re-sends a request at most three times after classify() returns 'retry'.
math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) returns True, so math.isclose treats any two amounts that differ only by floating-point error as equal.
On Python 3.11, S2 prints sum(items) == 1.0 -> False.
round_money_dec(1.005) returns Decimal('1.01').
round_money(2.675) returns 2.67, not 2.68.
round_money_dec rounds half-up to two decimals for every float input without raising an error.
classify({'code': 503}) returns 'fail'.
The CSV exporter writes amounts with round_money_dec.
Sorting with reverse=True keeps tied invoices in their original order: desc is [('INV-3', 200), ('INV-2', 200), ('INV-1', 100), ('INV-4', 100)].
On Python 3.10, S6 produces the same by_amount ordering.

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP


def round_money(x):
    return round(x, 2)


def round_money_dec(x):
    return Decimal(str(x)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)


for v in [2.675, 1.005, 0.125, 0.375, 10.0]:
    print(f"round_money({v}) -> {round_money(v)!r}")
    print(f"round_money_dec({v}) -> {round_money_dec(v)!r}")

print(f"round(3.5) -> {round(3.5)!r}")

S4.snippet:
def split_instalments(total_cents, n):
    base = total_cents // n
    rem = total_cents % n
    return [base + (1 if i < rem else 0) for i in range(n)]


print(f"split_instalments(1000, 3) -> {split_instalments(1000, 3)!r}")
print(f"sum(split_instalments(1000, 3)) -> {sum(split_instalments(1000, 3))!r}")
print(f"split_instalments(10, 4) -> {split_instalments(10, 4)!r}")
print(f"-7 // 2 -> {-7 // 2!r}")
print(f"-7 % 2 -> {-7 % 2!r}")
print(f"int(-7 / 2) -> {int(-7 / 2)!r}")
